records.title: Repurposing the orphan drug nitisinone synergizes with sorafenib to sensitize immunotherapy-refractory MSS-CRC via metabolic stress-driven STING activation.
records.abstract: Microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) remains broadly refractory to immune checkpoint blockade, underscoring the need for strategies that convert immunologically "cold" tumors into therapy-responsive states. Here, we identify 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), the rate-limiting enzyme in tyrosine catabolism, as a modulator of sorafenib sensitivity in MSS-CRC. Pharmacological inhibition of HPD by the FDA-approved orphan drug nitisinone synergized with sorafenib across patient-derived organoids, human PBMC-tumor co-cultures, and immunocompetent orthotopic models. Mechanistically, nitisinone imposes strict glutaminolysis dependency, whereas sorafenib disrupts cRaf-MEK-ERK signaling to trigger proteasomal cMYC degradation and transcriptional repression of GLS1, thereby ablating compensatory glutamine anaplerosis. This dual metabolic blockade creates a synthetic lethal trap, provoking irreversible mitochondrial collapse and mtDNA release, which activates the cGAS-STING pathway and drives intratumoral infiltration of cytotoxic NK and CD8+ T cells. Critically, ρ⁰ cells and STING-deficient models confirm mitochondrial damage as the "trigger" of cell death and STING as the "amplifier" of antitumor immunity. In TCGA MSS-CRC cohorts, a double-low glutamine/tyrosine metabolic signature was associated with prolonged survival, enhanced cGAS-STING signaling, and immune-hot tumor features, findings corroborated by single-cell RNA-seq analyses. Finally, the triple combination of nitisinone, sorafenib, and anti-PD-1 therapy achieved superior antitumor efficacy with favorable tolerability in vivo. Collectively, our findings delineate a metabolic-mitochondrial-STING axis and support repurposing nitisinone as a promising translational strategy to sensitize MSS-CRC to immunotherapy.

records.title: Bovine endometrial organoids show selective transcript-level responses to a sequential hormone, cAMP and interferon tau regimen.
records.abstract: The bovine endometrium responds to ovarian and conceptus-derived signals that are essential for early pregnancy establishment, yet available in vitro systems remain limited in their ability to combine controlled stimulation with sustained three-dimensional epithelial organisation. Here, we generated bovine endometrial organoids (EGOs) from endometrial cell fractions enriched in glandular fragments and evaluated their transcript-level response to a sequential differentiation and stimulation regimen including oestradiol, progesterone, cyclic adenosine monophosphate and interferon tau. EGOs were maintained in Matrigel under defined expansion and differentiation conditions and formed cystic structures lined by epithelial-like cells around a central lumen. Histology confirmed this epithelial-like cystic morphology, whereas representative confocal immunofluorescence performed with organoids from one uterus documented marker-associated signals. Quantitative PCR identified a selective transcriptional response, most consistently reflected by increased expression of canonical interferon tau-responsive genes, including ISG15, MX1, MX2, and OAS1Y. Additional transcripts showed more heterogeneous responses, whereas several expected hormone-associated genes did not differ clearly under the conditions evaluated. Because molecular readouts were assessed primarily at the transcript level and immunofluorescence comparisons were descriptive, these findings should be interpreted accordingly. Overall, organoids generated from gland-enriched bovine endometrial fractions formed epithelial-like cystic structures and showed selective transcript-level responses to the complete sequential differentiation and stimulation regimen.

records.title: Fluid-driven robotic micromanipulation for assembloid fabrication.
records.abstract: The assembly of cellular spheroids into spatially organized assembloids represents a transformative paradigm for modeling complex biological systems. However, the lack of standardized fabrication strategies fundamentally limits the precision and reproducibility of these models, hindering their widespread application. Here, we present a robotic micromanipulation platform-Fluid-Driven Tweezer with Visual Servo Control (FDT-VSC). By integrating multidimensional visual perception with microfluidic control, our system enables the gentle and programmable assembly of diverse cellular spheroids. Leveraging this platform, we achieve the bottom-up construction of structurally defined, heterogeneous multicellular tissues, and the programmed orchestration of multilineage models that recapitulate the complex microenvironments of early organogenesis. Crucially, the system improves consistency during the scalable fabrication of tumor-stroma assembloids, supporting reliable drug screening. These results demonstrate that FDT-VSC advances assembloid-based applications across modular tissue engineering, developmental biology, and drug discovery.

records.title: Human hair-bearing skin organoids reveal cell type-specific susceptibility and innate immune responses to herpes simplex virus 1.
records.abstract: Epithelial surfaces are the primary sites of lytic herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) infection following initial exposure or reactivation from latency. To model this complex environment, we used human hair-bearing skin organoids and combined single-cell spatial transcriptomics with imaging to map viral spread and host responses across skin architecture. Our data suggest delayed progression of the HSV-1 life cycle in epidermal keratinocytes and hair follicle cells compared to the dermis. Infection triggered spatially organized host responses, including induction of IER3 in papillary fibroblasts. In basal keratinocytes, IRF3 was up-regulated in both infected and neighboring uninfected cells, consistent with paracrine activation of antiviral signaling. Inflammatory responses were compartmentalized in a cell type-specific manner, with TNFSF9 (4-1BBL) induced in papillary fibroblasts and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) induced in keratinocytes. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays confirmed secretion of these cytokines and the TNF-α-responsive chemokines CXCL2 and CXCL10. CXCL2 expression was enriched in cells adjacent to TNF-α-expressing cells, highlighting spatial coordination of inflammatory signaling. While interferon-β reduced viral replication, TNF-α and 4-1BBL did not, suggesting that their primary role is to orchestrate immune cell recruitment and activation. These findings establish human hair-bearing skin organoids as a physiologically relevant model for investigating spatial host-HSV-1 interactions.

records.title: Protocol for generating human organoid tumor transplantation and immune-human organoid tumor transplantation models for glioblastoma research.
records.abstract: Glioblastoma research requires human models that preserve tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental interactions. Here, we present a protocol for generating the human organoid tumor transplantation (HOTT) model and its immunocompetent counterpart, the immune-HOTT (iHOTT) model. These platforms use direct-from-patient tumor cells engrafted into organoids to recapitulate the tumor microenvironment and, in the iHOTT system, autologous tumor-immune interactions. We describe steps for organoid generation, patient tumor dissociation, co-culture with autologous peripheral blood mononuclear cells, fluorescence-activated cell sorting, and downstream single-cell RNA sequencing. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Ge et al. and Baisiwala et al.1,2.

records.title: The Mechanical Properties of Spinal Cord Organoids Depend on Their Age and Composition.
records.abstract: Spinal cord organoids are valuable human in vitro models of development and disease. Many aspects of cell behavior and function in the spinal cord are regulated by mechanical signals, but the mechanical properties of human spinal cord organoids remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we quantify the elastic and viscoelastic properties of human spinal cord organoids at four ages (days 51, 87, 132, and 179) using microindentation. The average effective Young's modulus across all organoids was 731 ± 336 Pa, and stiffness increased with age (R2 = 0.49, p < 0.0001). Stress relaxation testing revealed pronounced viscoelasticity, with age-dependent increases most pronounced at short relaxation times and more modest at long relaxation times, suggesting that maturation selectively stiffens the short-time response while leaving long-time equilibrium stiffness largely unchanged. Immunohistological analysis revealed that neurofilament heavy chain (NFH) immunoreactivity increased with age and correlated significantly with effective Young's modulus, while glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) immunoreactivity, despite increasing with age, did not correlate with stiffness, suggesting that neuron maturation contributes to age-dependent stiffening. These findings establish quantitative mechanical properties for human spinal cord organoids, provide age-specific material parameters for computational modeling and synthetic neural interface design, and inform the design of experiments related to assembloid interactions and durotaxis in the developing central nervous system.

records.title: Artificial Cells and Biomimetic Cells: Intelligent Systems Driving a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery and Delivery.
records.abstract: The convergence of synthetic biology, materials science, and artificial intelligence drives a transformative shift in biopharmaceutical research, advancing from passive drug carriers to intelligent, programmable therapeutics. This review evaluates artificial and biomimetic cells as a framework that connects fundamental biological discovery with clinical translation. It examines five key technological pathways: membrane-engineered artificial cells, membraneless organelle (MLO) systems, multicompartmental artificial cells, protocell communication networks, and virtual cells. These platforms enable precise regulation of drug stability, targeting, biosynthesis, and adaptive responsiveness. Recent progress includes microenvironment-triggered release, logic-gated intercellular communication, and virtual cell-assisted high-throughput screening and toxicity prediction. Despite these advances, challenges remain in scalable manufacturing, long-term stability, and regulatory adaptation. The integration of closed-loop learning, interpretable models, and advanced biomanufacturing will be essential to position artificial and biomimetic cell systems at the forefront of next-generation precision medicine.

records.title: The Tenocyte from Atom to Cell: A Critical Multiscale Synthesis Linking Collagen Chemistry, Tissue Mechanics, Cell Mechanobiology and Mathematical Modelling.
records.abstract: The tenocyte builds, maintains, senses and degrades one of the most mechanically demanding extracellular matrices in vertebrates, yet the chemical, physical, biological and mathematical descriptions of this system have developed in largely separate literatures. This review examines the tenocyte-matrix unit as a single causal system spanning eight orders of magnitude in length, organised around five transitions: from collagen chemistry to molecular mechanics; from molecule to fibril and fascicle; from tissue loading to the cellular mechanical stimulus; from stimulus to transcription; and from cellular output back to matrix composition. At each transition, we weigh competing hypotheses, identify where evidence is decisive and where it remains correlative, and state the governing equations. We integrate advances from 2021-2026, including single-cell and spatial transcriptomic atlases of human tendons, the establishment of PIEZO1 as a causal regulator of tendon stiffness, and microstructurally derived constitutive models. We argue that tendon homeostasis is a closed-loop control problem, formalised as a mechanostat with an inverted-U dose-response, and that the recurrent pathologies of tendon-tendinopathy, ageing, diabetic stiffening and fibrotic healing are failures of this loop rather than of any single component. An open-source computational companion (tenocyte-virtual-cell) is introduced, and a prioritised research agenda closes the review.

records.title: Primary-Tumor Transcriptomic Signatures Associated with Circulating Tumor Cells Status in Breast Cancer: From CTC-Negative Remodeling to CTC-Associated Metastatic Programs.
records.abstract: Background/Objectives: Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) play a central role in metastasis by enabling tumor dissemination through the bloodstream. However, the molecular transition from CTC-negative (CTC-) to CTC-positive (CTC+) states and their associated systemic remodeling remain poorly understood. Methods: We performed a transcriptomic comparison between CTC+, CTC-, and healthy individuals using RNA-seq data and a bioinformatics pipeline. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were subjected to functional enrichment, protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis, survival modeling, and drug perturbation prediction to delineate the molecular determinants of CTC emergence and persistence. Results: Primary tumors from CTC+ patients exhibited distinct transcriptomic profiles characterized by the upregulation of genes involved in PI3K-Akt signaling, extracellular matrix organization, and chromatin regulation (e.g., HDAC1, JUN, KLK10), alongside the downregulation of immune activation pathways, including complement, B-cell receptor (BCR), and T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling. Multi-gene survival models derived from upregulated (KLK10, MEOX2, IRS4, RND2) and downregulated (ALDH3A1, PPP2R2B, IGF1R) hub genes significantly stratified patient outcomes (HR = 1.74-2.44, p < 0.01). In contrast, primary tumors from CTC- patients displayed early systemic transcriptional alterations relative to healthy controls, with 1700+ DEGs linked to MAPK/ERK and receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling pathways, suggesting pre-metastatic immune reprogramming even before CTC detection. Drug repurposing analysis identified Trichostatin A, BX-795, and Alvocidib as candidate compounds capable of reversing the CTC+ transcriptional signature. Conclusions: Rather than supporting a strictly binary view of CTC status, our findings are consistent with a transcriptional continuum of distinct yet partially overlapping primary-tumor transcriptional states associated with CTC- and CTC+ status, highlighting a molecular shift from immune suppression to epigenetic adaptation that facilitates hematogenous dissemination. The identified multi-gene prognostic panels and small-molecule candidates provide a foundation for CTC-targeted therapeutic strategies and early detection biomarkers in breast cancer.

records.title: Single-Cell Whole-Transcriptome Detection Expands the Observable RNA Space for AI Virtual-Cell Models.
records.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has supplied cell atlases and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled virtual-cell models with scalable, gene-level descriptions of cellular state. Yet prevalent poly(A)-based counting assays capture only part of the RNA landscape. Here, "single-cell whole-transcriptome detection" denotes sequencing-based efforts to detect a broader range of RNA biotypes than conventional poly(A)-based gene counting; no assay detects or quantifies every cellular RNA species without bias. We compare RNA-capture scope, transcript-structure resolution, temporal labeling, spatial context, and additional modalities as distinct measurement dimensions. From a biosensing perspective, analytical sensitivity, transcript coverage, throughput, and assay bias determine which signals are available to computational models. We then examine cell-state representations, regulatory networks, dynamics, perturbation prediction, and foundation models. Total-RNA assays reveal additional non-coding RNAs, long-read methods inform transcript structure, and temporal assays constrain RNA kinetics. Whether these signals improve prediction beyond conventional gene-count inputs requires matched, task-specific model comparisons. We distinguish molecular observability, statistical association, predictive performance, and causal validation, which requires appropriate interventions. We propose benchmarks controlling sequencing depth, cost, model architecture, and held-out samples while testing feature ablations, out-of-distribution performance, uncertainty calibration, and experimental outcomes. Together, high-throughput poly(A)-based profiling and broader RNA measurements provide complementary cellular breadth and regulatory depth.

records.title: Virtual cells: progress and challenges from mechanistic modeling to data-driven integration.
records.abstract: Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

records.title: Progress of metabolomics-centric multi-omics research in medicine.
records.abstract: Metabolomics reveals molecular changes at the metabolic level during biological processes. Recent advancements, particularly through integration with other omics and artificial intelligence (AI), are advancing metabolic data analysis and multi-omics interpretation. This review introduces a "metabolomics-centric" paradigm as a conceptual framework for multi-omics integration, positioning metabolic readouts as the functional anchor for interpreting genotype-phenotype relationships. It also chronicles the evolution and medical applications of integration technologies. Our discussion first traces the field's evolution from bulk to single-cell and spatial methodologies, next surveys integration strategies to uncover mechanistic insights, and finally examines how AI-driven multimodal data integration and AI-optimized metabolomics workflows tackle persistent biological and computational challenges. Looking forward, this review identifies the AI virtual cell as a pivotal future direction for metabolomics-based multi-omics integration, calling for increased attention to its development to simulate dynamic molecular phenotypic networks within a multi-omics context.

records.title: Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow.
records.abstract: Directed evolution consistently delivers engineered enzymes that facilitate diverse biocatalytic transformations. Despite advances in automation and high-throughput workflows, our ability to rapidly engineer novel enzymes is limited by our inability to thoroughly sample the vast protein design space. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) methods have alleviated this challenge to some degree, due to their ability to propose mutations based on learned patterns from complex protein data sets. However, the hidden logic of these AI-based methods can complicate our ability to reveal and exploit fundamental details of these enzymes. To complement these hidden-logic models, we present a structure- and physics-based workflow that mimics directed evolution in silico. This Virtual Protein EngineeR (referred to as ViPER) aims to simulate directed evolution by leveraging computational modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, in silico mutagenesis, and structure-based property evaluation to iteratively engineer an enzyme toward a desired target. In this work, we present a retrospective analysis to demonstrate ViPER's ability to efficiently navigate the complex protein-protein interfaces associated with the oligomerization of a ketoreductase (KRED) enzyme. In addition to successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds), this dynamics-based methodology identifies a distal mutation that was incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution. This work provides a novel foundation for computationally driven directed evolution efforts, opening the opportunity to simultaneously pursue and evaluate multiple evolutionary routes through a physics-based lens.

records.title: Evaluating generative models for structure-based drug discovery from de novo design to lead optimization.
records.abstract: Advances in protein structure prediction have created opportunities for structure-based drug design, yet translating structural knowledge into actionable small-molecule ligands remains difficult. Existing benchmarks often use simplified datasets and computational surrogates that poorly capture the heterogeneity and constraints of real-world drug discovery. We introduce MolGenBench, a comprehensive benchmark for de novo molecular generation and hit-to-lead optimization built on a large, structurally diverse dataset. Evaluation of 17 leading methods reveals persistent limitations, including weak virtual-screening performance, limited coverage of target-specific bioactive space, frequent high-risk structural motifs, poor target awareness, and reduced generalization to unseen proteins. Although some models improve three-dimensional conformation generation, they still struggle to produce active molecules reliably. MolGenBench provides standardized data, metrics, and analyses that connect structural prediction with practical molecular design and guide the development of more effective structure-based generative models.

records.title: Roads not taken: The mismatch between safety and regulation of plant breeding innovation.
records.abstract: Meeting global food security goals while reducing agriculture's environmental impact requires continued crop improvement and innovation. Advances in transgenesis, cisgenesis, and genome editing now enable increasingly precise genetic modification with risks comparable to those of conventional breeding, yet regulatory frameworks remain focused on the method used rather than the product. We highlight recent examples, including immune receptor transfer, cisgenesis-based disease resistance stacking, photosynthesis engineering, and AI-guided protein design, that illustrate innovations constrained by current regulatory approaches. A decisive shift toward science-based, proportionate, and product-focused regulation is needed so that improved crops are evaluated on the basis of their properties, not how they were made.

records.title: Structural mechanism of programmable gene integration by the R2 retrotransposon coupled with CRISPR-Cas9.
records.abstract: R2 retroelements are non-long-terminal-repeat retrotransposons that primarily insert into 28S ribosomal DNA loci across diverse eukaryotes. R2 elements home to their target sites through target-primed reverse transcription (TPRT), in which the R2 protein recognizes and nicks the target DNA to prime reverse transcription using an R2-encoding RNA as the template. The avian R2 system from Taeniopygia guttata (R2Tg) can insert a payload sequence within an RNA template into 28S ribosomal DNA loci in human cells. Here, we present cryo-electron microscopy structures of the R2Tg-template RNA-target DNA complex in the TPRT initiation state, both alone and bound to a Cas9-guide RNA complex. These structures provide mechanistic insights into R2Tg-mediated TPRT in its natural context and in the programmable gene integration system STITCHR (site-specific target-primed insertion through targeted CRISPR homing of retroelements). Furthermore, we combine these structural insights with computational protein design methods to engineer an enhanced STITCHR system.

records.title: Application of computational methods in the drug discovery and development of Alzheimer's disease.
records.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to cognitive decline. As the most common dementia, AD affects over 50 million individuals worldwide, with 10 million new cases each year. Despite many significant progresses in AD research fields, there is still no effective treatment. Advances in molecular modelling and artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm have facilitated the application of computational methods in AD drug development, offering advantages in terms of efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and resource conservation. These strategies, including molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulation, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, and de novo drug design, have been widely employed in the past decades. Additionally, AI pharmaceutical companies have revolutionized the traditional drug development pipeline such as AD biomarker discovery, accurate diagnosis and precision medicine, etc. This review offers a thorough summary of recent progresses in computational-based methodologies in the study of AD drug development, including the elucidation the pathological mechanism at the molecular level, target identification, target 3D structure prediction, lead compound discovery, de novo molecular generation, multi-target directed ligands, drug repurposing, biomarker discovery, etc., showing promising applications of molecular modelling and AI in the development of AD therapy.

records.title: Structure-Function Relationships of Cid1 Poly(U) Polymerase: Catalysis, Substrate Recognition, Engineering, and Applications.
records.abstract: RNA 3'-end modification is an important regulatory mechanism that influences RNA processing, stability, localization, function, and degradation. Beyond its biological roles, RNA 3'-end modification has become a valuable tool in biotechnology, enabling applications in RNA labelling, sequencing, engineering and oligonucleotide synthesis. Terminal nucleotidyltransferases are key enzymes responsible for template-independent nucleotide addition to RNA molecules. Among these enzymes, Schizosaccharomyces pombe Cid1, a poly(U) polymerase, has emerged as an important model for understanding RNA-specific terminal nucleotidyltransferase activity. Structural and biochemical studies have revealed how nucleotide recognition, metal-ion-dependent catalysis, RNA positioning, and conformational dynamics regulate Cid1-mediated uridylation. Recent advances in protein engineering, molecular simulation, machine learning, and generative protein design have further expanded Cid1 functionality, generating variants with improved activity, altered substrate specificity, and potential applications in enzymatic RNA synthesis. This review summarizes the biological functions, structural characteristics, catalytic mechanisms, protein engineering strategies, and emerging biotechnological applications of Cid1, as well as the remaining challenges, highlighting its potential as a programmable platform for RNA 3'-end functionalization and enzymatic RNA oligonucleotide synthesis.

records.title: Multimodal Biosensing for Liquid Biopsy: A Critical Analysis of Signal Complementarity, Data Fusion, Artificial Intelligence, and Clinical Translation.
records.abstract: Liquid biopsy provides minimally invasive access to diverse tumor-derived biomarkers, but their low abundance, biological variability, and complex matrices limit the reliability of single-mode biosensing. Multimodal biosensors address these challenges by combining complementary sensing mechanisms; however, multiple signals do not necessarily constitute meaningful data fusion or clinical benefit. This review critically evaluates multimodal liquid-biopsy biosensing at the signal, information, and computational/decision levels, focusing on whether additional modalities provide non-redundant analytical information. Molecular recognition, functional materials, signal engineering, integrated architectures, and computational methods are assessed alongside analytical validation, matrix effects, reproducibility, clinical-sample evidence, external validation, and AI maturity. A complementary framework distinguishes analytical, clinical, computational, and deployment readiness. Overall, most platforms remain at proof-of-concept or early validation stages, with limited evidence of externally validated data fusion or clinical utility. The review identifies the conditions required for multimodality to deliver genuine analytical value and outlines the methodological, computational, and clinical requirements for advancing toward reliable liquid-biopsy decision systems.

records.title: HPV-associated extracellular vesicles and the tumor microenvironment: mechanisms of immune modulation and translational implications.
records.abstract: Human papillomavirus infections are a major cause of cervical cancer and are also associated with several anogenital and oropharyngeal malignancies. Persistent infection with high-risk HPV types and sustained expression of viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 contribute to malignant transformation. Extracellular vesicles are increasingly recognized as important mediators of intercellular communication and can transfer proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and other regulatory molecules between cells. HPV-associated changes in EV cargo, such as viral transcripts, may influence immune and stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment. Experimental studies have implicated HPV-associated EVs in the regulation of dendritic cell function, macrophage polarization, T-cell responses, immune checkpoint signaling, chronic inflammation, and mechanisms related to viral persistence and immune evasion. Cell-based and preclinical studies also suggest that EVs released by HPV-positive tumor cells may contribute to related disorders including angiogenesis and metastatic progression. On the other hand, human studies have primarily provided observational evidence linking EV-associated molecular profiles with HPV status or disease characteristics. Beyond these mechanistic insights, a growing body of work explores the translational potential of EVs, including their use as liquid-biopsy biomarkers and as engineered delivery platforms such as Nefmut-based vesicles carrying HPV16 E7 that elicit protective CD8 + T-cell responses in preclinical models. This narrative review, with emphasis on tumor-immune interactions, and also discusses emerging diagnostic and therapeutic applications together with the methodological and clinical barriers that must be addressed before EV-based strategies can be translated into routine practice.

records.title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated tumor-nerve crosstalk: mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities.
records.abstract: Accumulating evidence indicates that solid tumors actively recruit peripheral nerves into the tumor microenvironment (TME), where the infiltrating nerves profoundly influence tumor initiation, progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance. Beyond classical neural signaling, extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as pivotal mediators of tumor-nerve communication. These nanoscale membrane-bound vesicles deliver oncogenic cargo (e.g., proteins and RNAs) that induces axonogenesis and reprograms neurons, thereby reshaping the neural niche to favor malignancy. EVs have also attracted growing attention for their important roles in coordinating the tripartite crosstalk among tumor cells, neurons, and immune cells, which fosters an immunosuppressive, pro-tumorigenic microenvironment. Furthermore, EVs orchestrate the glial, endothelial, and fibroblastic compartments, thereby embedding tumor-nerve communication within a broader multicellular network. In this review, we synthesize current insights into EV-mediated tumor-nerve crosstalk within the TME and evaluate the potential of EVs both as liquid-biopsy biomarkers for detecting perineural invasion and as therapeutic targets for disrupting pathological tumor innervation. Finally, we propose novel hypotheses and outline future directions for addressing the remaining challenges, with the aim of advancing tumor denervation therapies.

records.title: Syncytiotrophoblast differentiation defects drive ER stress and reprogram placental PSG1 glycosylation in preeclampsia.
records.abstract: During pregnancy, placenta-derived proteins such as pregnancy-specific glycoprotein 1 (PSG1) enter the maternal circulation, providing a window into placental health and enabling liquid biopsy strategies for monitoring pregnancy disorders. PSG1, a highly glycosylated protein secreted by syncytiotrophoblast (STB) cells, reflects trophoblast differentiation status. Circulating PSG1 levels are reduced in early-onset preeclampsia (PE), but how PSG1 glycosylation is altered in this condition remains unclear. Here, we show by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry that native PSG1 purified from healthy and early-onset PE pregnancies carries an O-linked glycan in its N domain in addition to diverse N-linked glycans. In PE, PSG1 N-glycans displayed a shift toward increased oligomannose structures and reduced sialylation. Induction of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress in primary STBs altered the glycosylation enzyme machinery, and single-nucleus transcriptomic data indicated a reduced contribution of mature STB populations in PE, consistent with an immature STB-like glycoprotein signature. Altered N-glycosylation increased binding to mannose and asialoglycoprotein receptors and cellular uptake, suggesting enhanced hepatic clearance as a possible explanation for reduced circulating PSG1 levels in PE. Our data link ER stress during STB differentiation to altered glycoprotein maturation and identify PSG1 glycosylation as a readout of a stress-impaired STB in PE. Glycan features of circulating placental proteins could therefore provide information beyond protein levels alone and complement liquid biopsy approaches.

records.title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Terahertz-Colorimetric Dual-Mode Metadevice Based on Metallic Nanonetworks for microRNA Panel Assays.
records.abstract: Early diagnosis and accurate staging are essential for improving treatment efficacy and clinical outcomes of pancreatic cancer (PC), but remain challenging because of limited early PC-specific biomarkers and high-performance detection methods. In this paper, we developed a machine learning (ML)-enhanced terahertz (THz)-colorimetric dual-mode metadevice based on metallic nanonetworks for multiplexed microRNA (miRNA) detection and early PC diagnosis. Clinical sample measurements and bioinformatics analysis identified miRNA-21, miRNA-1290, and miRNA-320a as candidate PC biomarkers. Target miRNAs triggered the assembly of DNA-functionalized Fe and Au nanoparticles (NPs) with PEI-modified CuS NPs into ternary Fe/Au/Cu nanonetworks, generating THz and colorimetric signals through their dielectric and peroxidase-like properties. This target-triggered assembly enabled three-miRNA panel analysis without enzyme-mediated nucleic acid amplification and achieved attomolar-level miRNA profiling. Six ML algorithms were integrated to develop predictive models for PC diagnosis and staging. Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) achieved diagnostic accuracies of 97.8% (95% CI: 88.2-99.9%) in the training cohort (n = 45) and 96.7% (95% CI: 82.8-99.9%) in the validation cohort (n = 30), with 100% sensitivity for early PC in both cohorts. Compared with CA19-9, CA125, and CEA, the multiplexed miRNA-based dual-mode metadevice showed higher efficacy (area under the curve, AUC: 1.00 vs 0.905), supporting its potential for clinical miRNA-based liquid biopsy.
